# Diagnosing Overheating on a 2001 Honda Civic EX: When Fans Won't Spin

You've replaced the head gasket, swapped out the thermostat, ECT sensor, water pump, and radiator cap, yet the engine is still overheating because the cooling fans remain dead. You even confirmed the fans can spin by jumpering power directly to the relay or switch. At this stage, you are likely staring at a wiring harness or control module issue rather than another mechanical component failure.

The fact that the fans engage when you apply direct voltage is a critical diagnostic clue. It confirms two things: the fan motors themselves are functional, and the ground path for the fans is intact (assuming your jumper setup bypassed the ground logic correctly). The problem lies entirely in the control circuitry that tells the fans when to activate.

On the 2001 Honda Civic EX, the cooling system relies on an Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) sensor located at the thermostat housing and a cooling fan control module (often integrated into the radiator shroud or near the firewall). The ECT sensor acts as a variable resistor; as coolant temperature rises, its resistance drops. The Powertrain Control Module (PCM) reads this resistance to determine engine heat load. If the PCM detects high resistance (cold reading) when the engine is actually hot, it will not trigger the fans.

Given that you have already replaced the ECT sensor, the next most likely culprit is the cooling fan control module itself or a blown fuse cutting power before it reaches the module. Start by checking the fuses in the under-hood fuse box. Look for fuses labeled "FAN," "A/C," or "PCM." A visual inspection won't always reveal an internal break, so use a multimeter to verify continuity when the engine is cold and off. If the fuse is good but power isn't reaching the module's input terminal under hot conditions, you have an open circuit in the wiring harness leading to the PCM.

Another common pitfall on these generations of Civics is corrosion at the connector pins for the ECT sensor or the fan control module. Even if the parts are new, oxidized contacts can prevent the signal from registering. Disconnect the battery negative terminal before probing any connectors. Inspect the terminals inside the plug for green oxidation or bent prongs. A simple application of electrical contact cleaner and a gentle wiggle of the connector while monitoring resistance values can sometimes resolve an intermittent signal drop that mimics a faulty sensor.

If the wiring checks out, the PCM might be receiving a valid signal but failing to output the control voltage to the fan module due to an internal failure. This is less common than a bad part, but it happens. In this scenario, swapping the PCM with a known-good unit (with the same VIN calibration) is the definitive test. However, given the cost of a new PCM versus a used one, weigh the trade-off carefully.

Since you haven't replaced the radiator yet, ensure there is no blockage restricting coolant flow to the upper hose near the thermostat housing. Sometimes a partially collapsed upper radiator hose can mimic fan failure by starving the engine of cooling capacity, causing rapid temperature spikes that confuse the PCM's logic before the fans even get a chance to ramp up. Inspect the hose for soft spots or internal delamination when the engine is cool.

Finally, if all electrical paths are clear and sensors are reading correctly, but the system still refuses to engage the fans, the issue may be a software calibration mismatch if you recently flashed the PCM or swapped ECU units. In rare cases, the fan relay inside the power distribution block near the battery could be stuck open. Trace the high-current path from the battery fuse directly to the fan motor connector; if there is voltage drop across this section under load, replace the relay or the main cooling fan assembly.

Your diagnostic journey has successfully eliminated mechanical failures and sensor faults. The remaining variables are strictly electrical: power delivery, signal integrity, and control logic. Systematically isolating these factors will point you to the exact failure mode without further random part replacement.
